stem: Your app sends the same 20k-token system prompt on every request, followed by a short user message. What cuts cost **and** latency the most?

choices.text: Enable prompt caching on the system prompt
choices.reason: The repeated prefix is read from cache: cache reads cost a small fraction of the base input price (0.1× on most models, lower on some newer ones) and processing time drops.

choices.text: Stream the response
choices.reason: Streaming changes how output **arrives**; it doesn't discount the 20k input tokens processed on every request.

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens`
choices.reason: `max_tokens` caps output length only; it has no effect on input cost or speed.

choices.text: Send requests through the Message Batches API
choices.reason: Batches are cheaper but asynchronous (most finish within an hour), so latency goes **up**, not down.

takeaway: A big prefix that repeats should be **cached**; streaming doesn't make input cheaper.
mnemonic: Same start, every time? Cache it.

diagram.caption: Only the new part is processed at full price.

stem: Each request contains tool definitions, a long unchanging system prompt, then a block with the current timestamp and the user's message. Where should the `cache_control` breakpoint go?

choices.text: On the timestamp-and-message block, so the whole prompt is cached
choices.reason: That block changes every request, so the prefix never matches again; put the breakpoint at the end of the static prefix, not on the varying block.

choices.text: On the last block of the system prompt
choices.reason: Correct: mark the last block whose prefix is identical across requests; the tools and system prompt before it are cached too.

choices.text: Move the timestamp to the very start of the prompt, then cache the rest
choices.reason: The cache is a prefix: a change early in the prompt invalidates everything after it, so nothing would ever hit.

choices.text: On the first tool definition only
choices.reason: At best this caches only the first tool (and it may fall below the minimum cacheable length); the long system prompt would still be processed at full price.

takeaway: Put static content **first** and the breakpoint on the **last identical block**; varying content goes after it.
mnemonic: Static first, breakpoint at the seam, changes after.

diagram.caption: Cache prefixes build in this order; a change invalidates that level and everything after it.

stem: An internal tool caches a large system prompt, but users often pause 20–40 minutes between requests, so almost every request pays for a new cache write. What helps?

choices.text: Nothing needed: cached prefixes stay valid for 24 hours after they're written
choices.reason: The default cache lifetime is **5 minutes**, which is why these requests keep missing.

choices.text: Add more cache breakpoints to cache each section separately
choices.reason: Up to 4 breakpoints let you cache sections separately; they don't make any entry live longer.

choices.text: Set `"ttl": "1h"` on `cache_control` to use the 1-hour cache duration
choices.reason: Correct: the 1-hour option exists for gaps longer than 5 minutes; its writes cost 2× base input instead of 1.25×.

choices.text: Trim the system prompt below the minimum cacheable length so it stops writing
choices.reason: A prompt shorter than the model's minimum cacheable length can't be cached at all, so you'd lose caching entirely.

takeaway: The cache lives **5 minutes** by default and is refreshed free on each hit; use `ttl: "1h"` when gaps are longer.
mnemonic: Five minutes by default; an hour if you set `ttl`.

stem: You're budgeting for a model released before Claude 4.7 and want a rough token estimate for a 70,000-character English document. Using the ratio in Anthropic's glossary, about how many tokens is it?

choices.text: About 70,000 tokens
choices.reason: That treats every character as a token. Tokens can be single characters, but for these models the glossary's rough ratio is about 3.5 English characters per token.

choices.text: About 20,000 tokens
choices.reason: Correct: on models before Claude 4.7, a token is about 3.5 English characters, so 70,000 ÷ 3.5 ≈ 20,000. The exact number depends on the model and the language.

choices.text: About 14,000 tokens
choices.reason: That assumes about 5 characters per token; the glossary puts a token on these models at approximately 3.5 English characters, so the count is higher.

choices.text: About 245,000 tokens
choices.reason: That multiplies by 3.5 instead of dividing: each token covers several characters, so there are fewer tokens than characters.

takeaway: On models before Claude 4.7, a token is roughly **3.5 English characters**; Claude 4.7 and later produce about 30% more tokens for the same text.

stem: A request to Claude Sonnet 5 (1M-token context window) has 990k input tokens and sets `max_tokens` to 64k. What happens?

choices.text: The API returns a 400 "prompt is too long" error before generating any output
choices.reason: That error is for input that **alone** exceeds the window. Here the 990k input fits; only input plus `max_tokens` is over.

choices.text: The API returns a validation error because input plus `max_tokens` exceeds the window
choices.reason: That was the behavior on models before Claude 4.5. On Claude 4.5 models and newer, the API accepts the request.

choices.text: The API drops the oldest turns first-in, first-out to make room for the output
choices.reason: Rolling first-in, first-out management is something chat interfaces such as claude.ai can do; in API requests previous turns are preserved completely.

choices.text: It's accepted; output may stop with `stop_reason: "model_context_window_exceeded"`
choices.reason: Correct: on Claude 4.5 models and newer, input plus `max_tokens` may exceed the window, and generation stops at the limit with this stop reason.

takeaway: Input alone over the window is a **400**; input plus `max_tokens` over it is accepted and may stop with `model_context_window_exceeded`.

diagram.caption: Only 10k tokens of output fit before the 1M-token window is full.

stem: An internal assistant now sends the whole 600k-token company wiki with every question, because the model has a 1M-token window. Answers have become less accurate. What best explains it?

choices.text: Accuracy and recall degrade as token count grows, so curate what's in the context
choices.reason: Correct: the docs call this context rot. More context isn't automatically better, so choosing what's in context is as important as the space available.

choices.text: The request exceeds the context window, so the API truncates the end of the wiki
choices.reason: 600k tokens is well inside a 1M-token window, so nothing has been cut off.

choices.text: Requests this long are billed at a long-context premium tier that lowers quality
choices.reason: Most 1M-window models bill long context at standard pricing (Claude Haiku 5.5 charges more over 100k tokens), and price doesn't change answer quality anyway.

choices.text: The API drops the oldest content first-in, first-out, so the system prompt is lost
choices.reason: That rolling behavior describes chat interfaces such as claude.ai; in API requests the content you send is preserved.

takeaway: A bigger window isn't a reason to fill it: accuracy and recall **degrade** as context grows (context rot).

stem: You cache a 300k-token document prefix on a 1M-token model. A teammate says the cache means those 300k tokens no longer take up context space, leaving room for 1M tokens of conversation. What's correct?

choices.text: Right: only uncached `input_tokens` count toward the context window limit
choices.reason: With caching, input is split across `input_tokens`, `cache_read_input_tokens` and `cache_creation_input_tokens`, and all three count toward the window.

choices.text: Partly: cached tokens count only on the first request, when the cache is written
choices.reason: Cache writes and cache reads both count: `cache_creation_input_tokens` and `cache_read_input_tokens` each count toward the window.

choices.text: Wrong: cached prefixes still occupy the window; caching only changes their price
choices.reason: Correct: the docs say cached prompt prefixes still occupy the context window. Caching changes the price of those tokens, not whether they count.

choices.text: Right, but only for a prefix in the system prompt; cached messages still count fully
choices.reason: Everything in the request counts toward the window, the system prompt included, whether or not it is cached.

takeaway: Caching changes the **price** of prefix tokens, not the **space** they take in the context window.

diagram.caption: Every part of the request counts toward the window, cached or not.

stem: A new teammate says: "Claude is just a next-word predictor, so it needs elaborate prompt tricks before it will follow instructions." Which answer reflects Anthropic's glossary?

choices.text: Pretraining on curated question-and-answer pairs is what teaches Claude to follow instructions
choices.reason: Pretraining uses a large **unlabeled** corpus, and pretrained models are not inherently good at answering questions or following instructions.

choices.text: Claude is a bare pretrained model, so fine-tune it through the Claude API before relying on it
choices.reason: Claude is not a bare language model: it is already fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant. The Claude API does not currently offer fine-tuning.

choices.text: RLHF only adds factual knowledge; instruction-following comes from pretraining on its own
choices.reason: RLHF trains the model to behave consistently with human preferences, including following instructions more effectively.

choices.text: Pretraining teaches next-word prediction; fine-tuning and RLHF made it a helpful assistant
choices.reason: Correct: pretrained models often need deep prompting skill, so fine-tuning and RLHF refine them; Claude has been fine-tuned to be a helpful assistant.

takeaway: Pretraining teaches **next-word prediction**; fine-tuning and RLHF are what make Claude follow instructions as an assistant.

stem: A slogan generator keeps producing near-identical taglines, and the team wants more variety. A teammate suggests lowering the temperature. Based on how temperature works, what would that do?

choices.text: Make outputs more varied, because lower temperature explores rarer, more surprising word choices
choices.reason: This is backwards: exploring rare, uncommon or surprising word choices is what **higher** temperature encourages.

choices.text: Make outputs more conservative, sticking closely to the most probable phrasing and answers
choices.reason: Correct: lower temperatures give more conservative, deterministic outputs; higher temperatures give more creative and diverse ones, which is the opposite of what they need.

choices.text: Make the replies shorter and more concise, but leave how varied they are unchanged
choices.reason: Temperature controls the randomness of the model's predictions, not how long the output is.

choices.text: Nothing noticeable, because temperature only changes the output of fiction prompts
choices.reason: Temperature controls the randomness of predictions in text generation generally; for fiction, higher temperature can vary the answers as well as the phrasing.

takeaway: Temperature controls **randomness**: lower means conservative and probable, higher means more diverse.

stem: A regression test sends the same prompt with temperature 0 and asserts the reply matches a saved string exactly. It fails now and then, though nothing in the prompt changed. What's the explanation?

choices.text: It's expected: even at temperature 0, identical inputs can give different outputs
choices.reason: Correct: the glossary says results are not fully deterministic even with temperature set to 0.

choices.text: Temperature 0 is fully deterministic, so something in the request itself must have changed
choices.reason: The glossary says the opposite: even with temperature 0, results will not be fully deterministic.

choices.text: Anthropic's API is non-deterministic, so run the test through a third-party cloud provider instead
choices.reason: The non-determinism applies both to Anthropic's first-party service and to inference through third-party cloud providers.

choices.text: Raise the temperature to 1 so that the outputs settle into one stable answer
choices.reason: Higher temperature leads to more creative and diverse outputs, so replies would vary **more**, not less.

takeaway: Don't rely on **identical** outputs: even at temperature 0, the API is not fully deterministic.

stem: Your ticket-summary prompt includes four examples, all short billing tickets written in the same style. Now Claude summarizes every ticket, even outage reports, like a short billing note. What should you change?

choices.text: Remove the examples and describe the format in words only
choices.reason: Examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and structure; the problem is which examples you chose, not having them.

choices.text: Add many more billing examples so the pattern is clearer
choices.reason: More of the same reinforces the unintended pattern. The guide suggests 3–5 examples, and they should be diverse.

choices.text: Use diverse examples, including outages, each in `<example>` tags
choices.reason: Correct: examples should be relevant, diverse enough that Claude doesn't pick up unintended patterns, and structured in `<example>` tags.

choices.text: Merge the examples into the instructions without tags so they read as rules
choices.reason: The guide says to wrap examples in `<example>` tags so Claude can tell them apart from instructions.

takeaway: Few-shot examples should be **relevant**, **diverse** and **tagged**; similar examples teach unintended patterns.

stem: A teammate calls `POST /v1/messages` over raw HTTP with an `Authorization: Bearer` API key and `content-type: application/json`, using a standard (single-workspace) key. Which required header is still missing?

choices.text: `x-api-key`
choices.reason: `x-api-key` is a legacy fallback for `Authorization`. It isn't required when `Authorization` is set.

choices.text: `anthropic-workspace-id`
choices.reason: It is required only with a multi-workspace API key and is optional for other keys.

choices.text: `anthropic-beta`
choices.reason: Beta headers are only for accessing beta features; a plain Messages request doesn't need one.

choices.text: `anthropic-version`
choices.reason: Correct: every request needs the API version header, for example `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01`.

takeaway: Raw HTTP requests need **auth**, `anthropic-version` and `content-type`; the SDKs send all three for you.

stem: Your backend is written in Ruby. You want an official, general-purpose client for the Messages API with built-in streaming, retries and error handling. What should you use?

choices.text: The OpenAI SDK compatibility layer, since there is no official Ruby SDK
choices.reason: There is an official Ruby SDK. Compatibility layers expose Claude through another framework's API and are not general-purpose Messages API clients.

choices.text: The Claude Agent SDK
choices.reason: The Agent SDK works at a higher level, providing the agent loop and tool execution, rather than being a client you call per request.

choices.text: The official Ruby client SDK
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic ships official client SDKs for Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby, each with built-in streaming, retries and error handling.

choices.text: Shell out to the `ant` CLI from Ruby
choices.reason: The `ant` CLI is for shell scripting and interactive use; the client SDKs are the general-purpose API clients.

takeaway: Official client SDKs cover **Python, TypeScript, C#, Go, Java, PHP and Ruby**.

stem: Your Python service wraps every SDK call in its own loop that retries 3 times on 5xx errors. Logs show a single failing request can reach the API up to 12 times. What explains this, and what's the setting to adjust?

choices.text: The SDK already retries transient errors twice by default; tune it with `max_retries`
choices.reason: Correct: each of your 4 tries makes up to 3 SDK attempts (1 + 2 retries), so 12 in total. `max_retries` configures or disables the SDK's retries.

choices.text: The SDK never retries on its own, so the API must be replaying failed requests server-side
choices.reason: The official SDKs do retry automatically: connection errors, rate limits and 5xx errors, twice by default.

choices.text: The SDK retries only 400 errors, so the extra attempts must come from elsewhere in your stack
choices.reason: The SDKs retry **transient** failures such as connection errors, rate limits and 5xx errors; a 400 means a problem with the request itself.

choices.text: The SDK ignores `retry-after` and retries at once; lower your own loop's delay to match
choices.reason: The SDKs retry with exponential backoff and honor the `retry-after` header when present.

takeaway: The SDKs retry transient failures **twice by default**; set `max_retries` rather than stacking a second retry loop.
mnemonic: SDK retries twice, so check before you wrap it.

stem: You are writing a raw server-sent events parser for streamed Messages responses. In what order do the events of a stream arrive (ignoring `ping` events)?

choices.text: `content_block_start` → `content_block_delta`s → `content_block_stop` → `message_start` → `message_delta`s → `message_stop`
choices.reason: `message_start` comes first, carrying a `Message` with empty `content`, before any content block.

choices.text: `message_start` → blocks (`content_block_start`, deltas, `content_block_stop`) → `message_delta`s → `message_stop`
choices.reason: Correct: this is the documented flow, and the last event is always `message_stop`.

choices.text: `message_start` → `message_delta`s → blocks (`content_block_start`, deltas, `content_block_stop`) → `message_stop`
choices.reason: The `message_delta` events, with top-level changes such as usage, come **after** the content blocks.

choices.text: `message_start` → `content_block_delta`s only, with no block start or stop → `message_delta`s → `message_stop`
choices.reason: Each content block also has a `content_block_start` before its deltas and a `content_block_stop` after them.

takeaway: A stream is `message_start` → content blocks (start, deltas, stop) → `message_delta` → `message_stop`.

diagram.caption: ping events may appear anywhere in the stream.

stem: While streaming a tool call, your code runs `JSON.parse` on every `input_json_delta` it receives and keeps getting parse errors. What should it do instead?

choices.text: Read the complete tool input from the `message_start` event, which arrives before the deltas
choices.reason: `message_start` carries a `Message` whose `content` is empty; the tool input arrives later, in deltas.

choices.text: Treat the tool input as a plain string throughout, since a string is the final type of `input`
choices.reason: The deltas are strings, but the final `tool_use.input` is always an **object**.

choices.text: Wait for a later `text_delta` event, which carries the finished tool input as one JSON object
choices.reason: `text_delta` updates text blocks. A `tool_use` block's input only arrives as `input_json_delta` partial JSON.

choices.text: Accumulate the partial JSON strings and parse once at `content_block_stop`, or use SDK helpers
choices.reason: Correct: the deltas are partial JSON strings. Accumulate them and parse once the `content_block_stop` event arrives, or let the SDKs do it for you.

takeaway: `input_json_delta` carries **partial** JSON: accumulate it and parse it at `content_block_stop`.

stem: Your hand-written stream parser throws whenever it sees an event type that isn't in its switch statement, and it has started crashing on some responses. What does the streaming guide say your code should do?

choices.text: Treat any unrecognized event type as a protocol error and retry the whole request
choices.reason: An unfamiliar event isn't an error: under the versioning policy, new event types may be added.

choices.text: Treat `ping` events as a sign that the connection has stalled, and reconnect when one arrives
choices.reason: Streams may include any number of `ping` events; they are a normal part of the stream.

choices.text: Handle unknown event types gracefully, because new event types may be added
choices.reason: Correct: in line with the versioning policy, new event types may be added, and your code should handle unknown types gracefully.

choices.text: Turn off streaming, since unexpected event types mean the stream itself is corrupted
choices.reason: Unknown event types are expected over time, not a sign of corruption; the guide says to handle them gracefully.

takeaway: Parsers must **tolerate** `ping` and unknown event types: new ones may be added.

stem: A Python job sets a very large `max_tokens` for long reports. It doesn't need text as it arrives, only the finished `Message`, but large non-streaming calls risk HTTP timeouts. What's the recommended approach?

choices.text: Call `.stream()` and then `.get_final_message()` to get the complete `Message`
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK streams internally, keeping the connection alive, and returns a `Message` identical to what `.create()` returns.

choices.text: Set `"stream": true` and read the response body as one JSON `Message`
choices.reason: With `"stream": true` the response arrives as server-sent events, not one JSON body, so you'd have to handle the events.

choices.text: Stream, but parse every server-sent event by hand to rebuild the `Message`
choices.reason: Possible, but unnecessary: the SDKs already accumulate the events and return the final `Message` for you.

choices.text: Split the report into many small requests so that none needs a large `max_tokens`
choices.reason: The guide's answer for large `max_tokens` values is streaming, which the SDKs require for these requests to avoid HTTP timeouts.

takeaway: Large `max_tokens` means **stream**, and `.get_final_message()` / `.finalMessage()` gives you the whole `Message` anyway.

stem: Your app base64-encodes a batch of scanned PDFs into a single 40 MB Messages API request, and the API responds with `413 request_too_large`. What does the error mean?

choices.text: The prompt has more tokens than the model's context window allows in a single request
choices.reason: 413 `request_too_large` is about the request's size against the endpoint's limit (32 MB for Messages), not its token count.

choices.text: The request is larger than the Messages endpoint's 32 MB maximum request size
choices.reason: Correct: Messages requests are limited to 32 MB, and exceeding the limit returns a 413 `request_too_large` error.

choices.text: Your organization hit its tokens-per-minute rate limit on the Messages endpoint
choices.reason: Rate limits cap requests and tokens per minute; a 413 is the request-size error.

choices.text: The same request would succeed on Amazon Bedrock, which accepts larger request bodies
choices.reason: Bedrock limits requests to 20 MB, which is **smaller** than the direct API's 32 MB.

takeaway: Messages requests max out at **32 MB**; bigger requests get 413 `request_too_large`.

stem: Your streaming client checks the HTTP status and treats 200 as success. A response returns 200, but partway through the stream an error with type `overloaded_error` arrives. How should you interpret it?

choices.text: Your API key is invalid or was revoked partway through streaming the response
choices.reason: Key problems are `authentication_error` (HTTP 401), and the request was already accepted with a 200.

choices.text: Your organization hit its rate limit while the response was being streamed
choices.reason: Rate limits are `rate_limit_error` (HTTP 429). `overloaded_error` means the API itself is temporarily overloaded.

choices.text: It can be ignored: a 200 status means the response completed successfully
choices.reason: When streaming, an error can occur **after** the API returns 200, so the status alone doesn't mean the response finished.

choices.text: A mid-stream error after a 200: the API is temporarily overloaded
choices.reason: Correct: streamed errors can follow a 200 response, and `overloaded_error` (529) can happen when the API has high traffic across all users.

takeaway: When streaming, a 200 isn't the end of error handling: errors such as `overloaded_error` can arrive **mid-stream**.

stem: Your research agent runs on Claude Opus 5.5. It runs for hours doing multistep deep research, and your evals at `max` effort still fall short. According to Anthropic's guide, what should you try next?

choices.text: Claude Haiku 5.5
choices.reason: Haiku 5.5 is for the lowest latency and price: real-time apps, high-volume processing and sub-agent tasks, not the highest capability.

choices.text: Claude Sonnet 5.5
choices.reason: Sonnet 5.5 is for speed and capability on everyday coding, agent and enterprise work, not for when Opus 5.5 at max effort falls short.

choices.text: Claude Fable 5.1
choices.reason: Correct: if evals at `xhigh` or `max` effort still fall short on demanding reasoning or long-horizon agentic work, the guide says to move to Claude Fable 5.1.

choices.text: Lower effort to `medium` on Claude Opus 5.5
choices.reason: Effort trades intelligence for latency and cost, so lowering it gives up capability, the opposite of what these evals need.

takeaway: Start most workloads on **Opus 5.5**; move to **Fable 5.1** when evals at the highest effort still fall short.

stem: A high-volume, simple classification subtask runs on Claude Opus 5.5 at its default effort. Quality is fine, but it's slower and costlier than it needs to be. Which change fits the effort guidance?

choices.text: Send `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` to skip reasoning
choices.reason: On Claude Opus 5.5 adaptive thinking is always on; requests that set `thinking: {"type": "disabled"}` return a 400 error at every effort level.

choices.text: Raise effort to `xhigh`
choices.reason: `xhigh` is for long-running agentic and coding tasks and spends **more** tokens, which is the wrong direction here.

choices.text: Set effort to `"adaptive"`
choices.reason: `adaptive` is a thinking mode, not an effort level; effort values are `low`, `medium`, `high`, `xhigh` and `max`.

choices.text: Set `output_config.effort` to `low`
choices.reason: Correct: `low` is the most efficient level, for simpler tasks that need the best speed and lowest costs, such as subagents. It gives significant token savings with some capability reduction.

takeaway: Effort trades thoroughness for speed and cost on **one model**: use `low` for simple, speed-sensitive work.
mnemonic: Simple and fast? Turn effort down.

stem: A job on Claude Sonnet 4.5, which supports only manual extended thinking, sets `budget_tokens` to 48,000 for a hard analysis task. Some requests fail with timeouts. What does the extended thinking guide recommend?

choices.text: Use batch processing, which the guide advises for thinking budgets above 32k
choices.reason: Correct: thinking beyond 32k tokens makes long-running requests that can hit system timeouts and open-connection limits, so the guide says to use batch processing.

choices.text: Switch to `thinking: {"type": "adaptive"}` on the same model to avoid the timeouts
choices.reason: Adaptive thinking isn't available on models that support only extended thinking; `type: "adaptive"` returns a 400 error there.

choices.text: Set `budget_tokens` to 512 so that thinking finishes well before any timeout
choices.reason: The minimum budget is 1,024 tokens; the API rejects smaller values.

choices.text: Set `budget_tokens` above `max_tokens` so that thinking can finish sooner
choices.reason: `budget_tokens` must be less than `max_tokens` (except with interleaved thinking), because thinking tokens count toward `max_tokens`.

takeaway: Bigger thinking budgets cost **latency**; above 32k tokens, use batch processing to avoid timeouts.

stem: A synchronous workload on Claude Sonnet 5.5 ($2 / input MTok, $10 / output MTok) uses 10M input tokens and 2M output tokens a day, with no caching. What is the daily cost at base prices?

choices.reason: That bills all 12M tokens at the $2 input rate. Output has its own price: $10 per MTok on Claude Sonnet 5.5.
Correct: 10 MTok × $2 = $20 for input, plus 2 MTok × $10 = $20 for output, so $40 a day.
That's half of $40, the Batch API's 50% discount, which doesn't apply to synchronous requests.
That swaps the prices, billing input at $10 and output at $2. Input is the cheaper side: $2 per MTok on Claude Sonnet 5.5.

takeaway: Cost = input MTok × input price + output MTok × output price; output tokens cost **5×** input on Sonnet 5.5.

diagram.caption: Output is 1/6 of the tokens but half the bill.

stem: You're moving a pipeline from Claude Sonnet 4.5 to Claude Fable 5.1 and plan to reuse last quarter's token counts to budget costs and check context fit. What does the token counting guide advise?

choices.text: Reuse them: a prompt has the same token count on every model
choices.reason: Claude Fable 5.1 uses the tokenizer introduced with Claude Opus 4.7, and a prompt counts roughly 30% higher on it than on earlier models.

choices.text: Multiply the old counts by exactly 1.3
choices.reason: The increase is roughly 30%, but the exact increase depends on the content, so a fixed multiplier is only a guess.

choices.text: Avoid the token counting endpoint, because each call is billed as input tokens
choices.reason: Token counting is free to use; it is only subject to its own requests-per-minute rate limits.

choices.text: Recount the prompts with the token counting API, passing the new model's ID
choices.reason: Correct: the endpoint counts under the tokenizer of the `model` you pass, and the guide says not to reuse older models' counts for costs or context fit.

takeaway: Token counts depend on the **model's tokenizer**: recount with `count_tokens` for the model you're moving to.

stem: A web dashboard shows progress updates that your server pushes while a long Claude job runs. The browser never needs to send messages back on that channel. Which browser API fits best?

choices.text: A WebSocket, because only WebSockets let a server push data to the browser
choices.reason: Server-sent events also deliver data from server to client, over a persistent HTTP connection; WebSockets aren't the only way to push.

choices.text: Server-sent events through `EventSource`, a one-way stream from server to page
choices.reason: Correct: server-sent events are unidirectional, server to client, which makes `EventSource` an excellent choice when the client doesn't need to send data back.

choices.text: `EventSource`, with the page sending its replies back over that same connection
choices.reason: Unlike WebSockets, server-sent events are unidirectional: messages are delivered only from the server to the client.

choices.text: A new HTTP request every second that polls the server until the job has finished
choices.reason: An `EventSource` opens a persistent connection, and the server sends events over it as they happen, so the page doesn't keep asking.

takeaway: Server-to-client only? Use **server-sent events** (`EventSource`); WebSockets are for when the client must send messages too.

stem: Your browser-based voice assistant streams audio chunks to your server while the server streams Claude's replies back, all on one long-lived connection. It needs wide browser support today. Which browser API fits best?

choices.text: WebTransport, because it's the simplest option and has the widest browser support
choices.reason: WebTransport has features WebSockets lack, but it's more complex to use and its cross-browser support isn't as wide.

choices.text: `WebSocketStream`, the standard Promise-based interface that every engine supports
choices.reason: `WebSocketStream` handles backpressure, but it's non-standard and currently supported in only one rendering engine.

choices.text: The `WebSocket` interface, which opens a two-way session between browser and server
choices.reason: Correct: the WebSocket API opens a two-way interactive session, so you can send messages and receive responses without polling, with good browser and server support.

choices.text: Repeated HTTP requests from the browser that poll the server for each new reply chunk
choices.reason: With the WebSocket API you can send messages to a server and receive responses without having to poll the server for a reply.

takeaway: Both sides send on one connection? Use **WebSockets**; the `WebSocket` interface is the stable, widely supported choice.

stem: Each tab of your app opens an `EventSource` stream from `app.example.com` to show Claude's replies. The site is served over HTTP/1.1, and users with many tabs open find that new tabs just hang. What explains it, and what's the fix?

choices.text: Without HTTP/2, a browser allows only 6 SSE connections per domain; serve the streams over HTTP/2
choices.reason: Correct: when not used over HTTP/2, SSE is limited to 6 open connections per browser + domain, across all tabs. Over HTTP/2 the limit is negotiated (default 100).

choices.text: Each tab has its own cap of 6 connections, so one tab must be opening too many streams; merge them
choices.reason: The limit is per browser + domain and shared across all tabs, so many tabs with one stream each reach it together.

choices.text: Add a short `retry:` field to the stream so that hanging tabs reconnect and grab a free slot sooner
choices.reason: `retry` only sets how long the browser waits before reconnecting after a lost connection; it doesn't raise the connection limit.

choices.text: Wait for Chrome and Firefox to raise the cap, which both browsers plan to do in an upcoming release
choices.reason: The issue has been marked "Won't fix" in Chrome and Firefox, so the fix is on your side: serve the streams over HTTP/2.

takeaway: Over HTTP/1.1, SSE shares a cap of **6 connections per browser + domain**; serve streams over **HTTP/2**.

stem: Your runtime has no `EventSource`, so you're writing your own parser for a `text/event-stream` response. Which two rules of the event stream format must it follow?

choices.text: Treat every line as its own message, since each line of the stream is one complete event
choices.reason: Messages are separated by a **pair** of newlines, and one message can span several lines of fields.

choices.text: End a message at a blank line: messages are separated by a pair of newlines
choices.reason: Correct: each message is a block of text terminated by a pair of newline characters.

choices.text: Read a line that starts with a colon as the name of the event's type
choices.reason: A line that starts with a colon is in essence a comment, and is ignored; the type comes from the `event` field.

choices.text: Join consecutive `data:` lines of one message, with a newline between each
choices.reason: Correct: when consecutive lines begin with `data:`, they're concatenated, with a newline character inserted between each one.

choices.text: Treat `retry` as the number of reconnect attempts to make before giving up
choices.reason: `retry` is the reconnection time in milliseconds; a non-integer value is ignored.

takeaway: SSE messages end at a **blank line**; consecutive `data:` lines join with newlines, and lines starting with `:` are comments.

stem: Your browser code sets `evtSource.onmessage`, and the network panel shows events arriving, but the handler never runs. Every event in the stream has an `event:` field, such as `event: content_block_delta`. What's wrong?

choices.text: The `EventSource` needs `withCredentials: true` before it can deliver any events to the page
choices.reason: `withCredentials` only says whether cross-origin (CORS) credentials are sent; the events are already arriving.

choices.text: Add a `message` listener with `addEventListener`, which receives events of every type
choices.reason: A `message` listener catches events with no `event` field (or `event: message`); it won't trigger on other event types.

choices.text: The connection's `readyState` is `CLOSED`; call `close()`, then open a new `EventSource`
choices.reason: Events are reaching the page, so the connection is open; `close()` would end it and set `readyState` to `CLOSED`.

choices.text: Named events fire under their own names; use `addEventListener("content_block_delta")`
choices.reason: Correct: if a message has an `event` field, the event fired has that name and needs its own listener; `onmessage` handles messages without one.

takeaway: `onmessage` only sees **unnamed** events; listen for named SSE events with `addEventListener(name, ...)`.

stem: Your page uses `EventSource` to show a generated report. After the last event the server closes the connection, then the browser connects again and the server generates the whole report a second time. What should the page do?

choices.text: Call `evtSource.close()` at the final event: a closed connection is restarted by default
choices.reason: Correct: by default, if the connection between the client and server closes, it's restarted. The `.close()` method terminates it.

choices.text: Have the server send `retry: 0` at the end of the stream, so the browser knows not to reconnect
choices.reason: `retry` sets the reconnection wait in milliseconds after a lost connection; it changes when the browser reconnects, not whether.

choices.text: Have the server end the stream with a comment line, which tells the browser the stream is complete
choices.reason: A line starting with a colon is a comment and is ignored; servers send comments as keep-alives, not as end markers.

choices.text: Remove the `id` field from events, because the last event ID is what makes the browser reconnect
choices.reason: `id` sets the `EventSource` object's last event ID value; restarting a closed connection is the default either way.

takeaway: `EventSource` **restarts closed connections by default**; call `close()` when the stream is truly finished.

stem: Your server relays Claude's output to the browser over server-sent events. While a slow tool runs, no events are sent for a minute, and a proxy in between drops the idle connection. What's the standard fix within the event stream format?

choices.text: Have the browser send heartbeat messages to the server over the `EventSource` connection
choices.reason: Server-sent events are a one-way connection, so the client can't send events to the server on it.

choices.text: Send a `retry:` field so that the proxy waits longer before it closes an idle connection
choices.reason: `retry` is the browser's reconnection time after a lost connection; it doesn't stop an idle connection being dropped.

choices.text: Have the server send a comment line (one starting with `:`) periodically as a keep-alive
choices.reason: Correct: a line starting with a colon is a comment the client ignores, and a server can send one periodically to keep the connection alive.

choices.text: Change the response's MIME type to `application/json` so proxies treat it as a normal reply
choices.reason: The server must respond to an event stream using the MIME type `text/event-stream`.

takeaway: Keep idle SSE streams alive with periodic **comment lines** (starting with `:`), which clients ignore.

stem: Your team is replacing hand-written HTTP calls to the Claude API with an official client SDK. Which three things will the SDK take care of for you?

choices.text: Sending the auth, `anthropic-version` and `content-type` headers
choices.reason: Correct: automatic header management (authentication, `anthropic-version`, `content-type`) is one of the listed SDK benefits.

choices.text: Sending `anthropic-workspace-id` automatically for keys that need it
choices.reason: The SDK sends the auth, version and content-type headers; you pass `anthropic-workspace-id` yourself when your key needs it.

choices.text: Retrying failed requests and enforcing request timeouts
choices.reason: Correct: built-in retry logic and request timeouts and connection management are listed SDK benefits.

choices.text: Raising your organization's rate limits after repeated 429 errors
choices.reason: Limits are set by usage tier; for higher limits you use **Request tier increase** on the Console's Rate limits page.

choices.text: Following `next_page` cursors through list endpoint results
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK provides an auto-paginating iterator that follows `next_page` for you (forward only).

choices.text: Splitting Messages requests over 32 MB so they avoid a 413 error
choices.reason: 32 MB is the API's maximum request size for Messages; larger requests get a 413 `request_too_large` error.

takeaway: SDKs add **headers, retries, timeouts, types, streaming and auto-pagination**; workspace IDs, limits and request size stay your job.

stem: Your service switches from a single-workspace API key to a key with access to several workspaces. Requests go through an official client SDK. What must your code now add to each request?

choices.text: Nothing: the SDK reads the workspace from the key and sends the header for you
choices.reason: The SDK sends the auth, version and content-type headers; you pass `anthropic-workspace-id` yourself when your key needs it.

choices.text: An `anthropic-workspace-id` header naming the workspace the request runs in
choices.reason: Correct: `anthropic-workspace-id` is required with a multi-workspace API key, and the SDK leaves that header to you.

choices.text: An `x-api-key` header, which picks a workspace when sent with `Authorization`
choices.reason: `x-api-key` is a legacy fallback for `Authorization` that carries your API key; it doesn't select a workspace.

choices.text: An `anthropic-beta` header, since multi-workspace keys are still a beta feature
choices.reason: Beta headers are for beta features. A request picks its workspace with `anthropic-workspace-id`, required with multi-workspace keys.

takeaway: Multi-workspace keys need **`anthropic-workspace-id`** on each request; the SDK doesn't add it for you.

stem: A chat endpoint creates its Python client with `Anthropic(timeout=20.0)` so that users fail fast. When the API is slow, users still wait about a minute before they see an error. Why, and what should you change?

choices.text: A float `timeout` is ignored; only an `httpx2.Timeout` object replaces the 10-minute default
choices.reason: `timeout` accepts a float or an `httpx2.Timeout` object, so `timeout=20.0` does set a 20-second limit.

choices.text: `timeout` covers only streaming calls; non-streaming ones keep the default 10-minute limit
choices.reason: The `timeout` option sets the default for all requests on the client, or can be overridden per request.

choices.text: The API answers slow requests with a 504 after 60 s, and a client timeout can't end them sooner
choices.reason: On timeout the SDK itself raises `APITimeoutError`; the 20-second limit applies, but each timed-out attempt is retried.

choices.text: Timed-out requests are retried twice by default; lower `max_retries` for this client
choices.reason: Correct: requests that time out are retried twice by default, so three 20-second attempts add up to about a minute. `max_retries` configures this.

takeaway: SDK timeouts are **retried twice** by default, so the worst-case wait is about the timeout × 3; tune `max_retries` too.

stem: For each Messages call, your Python service must log one of the response headers along with the reply, but `client.messages.create()` returns only the parsed `Message`. What's the supported way to get both?

choices.text: Read `message._request_id`, which exposes every response header on the returned object
choices.reason: `_request_id` carries the value of the `request-id` response header only, not every header.

choices.text: Name the header in `extra_headers`, so that its value gets copied into the returned `Message`
choices.reason: `extra_headers` sends extra **request** headers; it doesn't copy response headers into the result.

choices.text: Call `client.messages.with_raw_response.create()`, read `.headers`, then call `.parse()`
choices.reason: Correct: `.with_raw_response` returns the raw response, headers included, and `.parse()` gives the object `messages.create()` would have returned.

choices.text: Use `with_streaming_response` without a context manager, so the headers stay readable
choices.reason: `.with_streaming_response` requires a context manager, so that the response is reliably closed.

takeaway: Need headers too? Use **`.with_raw_response`**, then `.parse()` for the usual `Message`.

stem: A cleanup script calls `client.messages.batches.list(limit=20)` and loops over the result's `.data`. Your account has hundreds of batches, but the script only ever sees 20. What's the simplest fix with the Python SDK?

choices.text: Read `last_id` from the first page, which holds the total number of batches
choices.reason: `last_id` is the cursor for fetching the next page, not a count of batches.

choices.text: Loop over the `list()` call itself; the SDK fetches more pages as needed
choices.reason: Correct: list methods are paginated, and iterating with `for` (or `async for`) automatically fetches more pages as needed.

choices.text: Call `has_next_page()` first, which loads every remaining item into `.data`
choices.reason: `.has_next_page()` only tells you whether another page exists; `.get_next_page()` fetches it.

choices.text: Switch to the async client, whose `list()` returns every page in one call
choices.reason: The async client paginates too; you iterate it with `async for`, which fetches more pages as needed.

takeaway: Iterate the list call itself: SDK **auto-pagination** fetches the following pages for you.

stem: Your raw HTTP pager works for `GET /v1/sessions`: it passes each `next_page` back as `page` until `next_page` is `null`. Reused for `GET /v1/models`, it stops after the first page, though more models exist. Why?

choices.text: The Models API returns every model in a single response, so there's no further page to fetch
choices.reason: List endpoints return results in pages, the Models API included; it just uses a different cursor scheme.

choices.text: `next_page` appears only when you also pass `order=desc`, which the Models API requires
choices.reason: `order` sets the sort direction on endpoints that support sorting; it doesn't decide whether `next_page` is returned.

choices.text: The Models API pages backward only, so your pager has to follow `prev_page` instead
choices.reason: Only `GET /v1/sessions` returns `prev_page`; on other list endpoints the field is absent.

choices.text: Models uses `after_id`/`before_id` and returns `has_more` and `last_id`, not `next_page`
choices.reason: Correct: Message Batches, Models and several Admin API endpoints take `after_id` and `before_id`, and return `has_more`, `first_id` and `last_id`.

takeaway: Not every list endpoint pages alike: Models and Batches use **`after_id` + `has_more`**, not `page`/`next_page`.

stem: Your code enables two betas by sending two separate `anthropic-beta` headers. Both features work on the Claude API, but after you move to Claude on Google Cloud, only one of them takes effect. What should you change?

choices.text: Put both beta names in one `anthropic-beta` header, separated by a comma
choices.reason: Correct: Google Cloud reads only one `anthropic-beta` header and ignores the rest, so list every beta in one comma-separated header.

choices.text: Move the beta names into an `anthropic_beta` array in the JSON request body
choices.reason: The body's `anthropic_beta` array is for Bedrock's InvokeModel API; Google Cloud takes beta names in the `anthropic-beta` header.

choices.text: Rename both betas, because Google Cloud uses its own platform-specific beta names
choices.reason: Beta names are the same on every platform that accepts them, though not every platform accepts every beta.

choices.text: Send each beta in a separate request, since only one beta can apply per request
choices.reason: You can use multiple betas in one request by listing all the names in the header, separated by commas.

takeaway: Several betas? Send **one** `anthropic-beta` header with comma-separated names; Google Cloud ignores extra copies.

stem: After a teammate edits the beta list in a raw HTTP client, every request fails with a 400 `invalid_request_error` whose message begins "Unexpected value(s)" and names the `anthropic-beta` header. What's the most likely cause?

choices.text: The API is overloaded, so the request should be retried with exponential backoff
choices.reason: The error names the `anthropic-beta` header: the API rejected a value in your request, which a retry would send again.

choices.text: The `anthropic-version` header was dropped from the request during the edit
choices.reason: The message names the `anthropic-beta` header, which is what the API returns a 400 about for an invalid beta name.

choices.text: A beta name is misspelled, or your organization lacks access to that beta
choices.reason: Correct: an invalid beta name, or a beta your organization doesn't have access to, returns a 400 that names the `anthropic-beta` header.

choices.text: Betas can't be combined, so adding a second name made the whole header invalid
choices.reason: Multiple betas are allowed: list them comma-separated in one header, or send the header more than once.

takeaway: A 400 naming `anthropic-beta` means a **wrong or inaccessible beta name**; use the exact documented name.

stem: Your raw HTTP client calls `POST /v1/sessions` with auth, `anthropic-version` and `content-type` headers, and the calls fail. The same request made with the SDK's `client.beta.sessions` works. What is the raw client missing?

choices.text: A `betas` field in the JSON body that lists `managed-agents-2026-04-01`
choices.reason: `betas` is the SDK's parameter; over raw HTTP the Claude API takes beta names in the `anthropic-beta` header.

choices.text: The `anthropic-beta: managed-agents-2026-04-01` header, on every request
choices.reason: Correct: `/v1/agents`, `/v1/sessions` and `/v1/environments` need `managed-agents-2026-04-01` on every request; `client.beta` adds it for you.

choices.text: The `agent-memory-2026-07-22` header, which also covers Sessions endpoints
choices.reason: `agent-memory-2026-07-22` is for `/v1/memory_stores`, where it replaces `managed-agents-2026-04-01`; sending both there returns a 400.

choices.text: Nothing in its headers: the Sessions API can only be called through an SDK
choices.reason: The SDK adds endpoint-specific beta headers automatically; you add them yourself only when making raw HTTP requests.

takeaway: Beta endpoints such as Sessions need their **endpoint-specific beta header** on every raw request; `client.beta` adds it for you.

stem: Your integration sends `anthropic-version: 2023-06-01` and validates every response against a strict schema that rejects anything unexpected. Which two kinds of change can Anthropic still make under that same version?

choices.text: Adding new values to the output, such as extra fields in a response
choices.reason: Correct: within a version Anthropic may add values to the output, so a schema that rejects anything unexpected can break.

choices.text: Removing an existing input parameter that your requests still send
choices.reason: For a given version, Anthropic preserves existing input parameters.

choices.text: Renaming an existing output field that your response parser reads
choices.reason: For a given version, Anthropic preserves existing output parameters.

choices.text: Adding new variants to enum-like values, such as stream event types
choices.reason: Correct: Anthropic may add new variants to enum-like output values, for example streaming event types.

choices.text: Making an existing optional input parameter required on every request
choices.reason: Within a version Anthropic preserves existing input parameters; the input change it may make is adding **optional** inputs.

takeaway: A version keeps existing parameters, but **outputs and enum values can grow**: parse responses tolerantly.

stem: Integration tests should send the app's Claude calls to a local mock server at `http://localhost:8083`. The app builds its client with a bare `Anthropic()`, and you don't want to change that code. What should the test environment set?

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug`, so the SDK sends its requests through a local debug server
choices.reason: `ANTHROPIC_LOG` (`debug` or `info`) turns on the SDK's logging through Python's `logging` module; it doesn't change where requests go.

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY=localhost:8083`, since the key's value picks the host to call
choices.reason: `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` is the default source of the API key the client sends, not of the host it calls.

choices.text: A `default_headers` entry that replaces `anthropic-version` with the mock's address
choices.reason: Default headers change request headers, and the SDK warns that overriding them can cause undefined behaviour; they don't change the URL.

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL=http://localhost:8083`, which the client uses for `base_url`
choices.reason: Correct: the client's `base_url` can come from the `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` env var, so the unchanged `Anthropic()` call targets the mock server.

takeaway: Point the SDK at another host with **`ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`** (or `base_url`); `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY` supplies the key.

stem: Your streaming handler saves `stop_reason` from the `message_start` event. Your dashboard now shows `stop_reason` as `null` for every streamed response, though the replies look complete. What's wrong?

choices.text: It's `null` in `message_start`; read `stop_reason` from the `message_delta` event
choices.reason: Correct: when streaming, `stop_reason` is `null` in the initial `message_start` event, provided in `message_delta`, and absent from other events.

choices.text: A `null` stop reason means Claude refused, so route these requests to a fallback model
choices.reason: A refusal is reported as `stop_reason: "refusal"`; `null` is just the initial value in `message_start`.

choices.text: The streams are being cut off early; retry each request until a `stop_reason` is set
choices.reason: The replies are complete. `stop_reason` is always `null` in `message_start`, so a retry would show the same.

choices.text: Read `stop_reason` from the final `message_stop` event, which is where it's reported
choices.reason: `stop_reason` is provided in the `message_delta` event, and not in any other event, `message_stop` included.

takeaway: When streaming, take `stop_reason` from **`message_delta`**; it's `null` in `message_start`.

stem: Your Python test suite mocks HTTP calls with `respx`, which patches `httpx`. The mocks work for your other clients, but the Anthropic SDK's requests aren't intercepted and go out to the network. What's the documented fix?

choices.text: Pass a plain `httpx.Client` as `http_client`, so the SDK sends through the patched library
choices.reason: `http_client` must be an `httpx2` client; passing a client from the separate `httpx` package raises a `TypeError`.

choices.text: Set `ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug`, which routes the SDK's traffic through the standard `logging` module
choices.reason: `ANTHROPIC_LOG` enables the SDK's logging; it doesn't change how or where requests are sent.

choices.text: Call `httpx2.alias_httpx()` once at startup, before anything else imports `httpx`
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK sends with `httpx2`, so tools that patch `httpx` don't see its requests by default; `alias_httpx()` makes `import httpx` resolve to `httpx2`.

choices.text: Set `max_retries=0`, because the SDK's retried requests skip any mocks you have installed
choices.reason: `max_retries` configures automatic retries; the mocks miss because the SDK uses `httpx2`, not `httpx`.

takeaway: The Python SDK sends with **`httpx2`**: tools that patch `httpx` need `httpx2.alias_httpx()` called first.

stem: A production Python service intermittently misbehaves when calling Claude. You want the SDK's own log output, without editing any code. What should you set before the service starts?

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL`, pointed at a logging proxy that ships inside the SDK
choices.reason: `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` sets the base URL requests go to; the SDK's logging is turned on with `ANTHROPIC_LOG`.

choices.text: `ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug`, which turns on the SDK's logging via Python's `logging`
choices.reason: Correct: the SDK uses the standard library `logging` module, and setting `ANTHROPIC_LOG` to `debug` or `info` enables it.

choices.text: `max_retries=0` on the client, so the SDK prints each failure it would have retried
choices.reason: `max_retries` configures or disables automatic retries; it isn't a logging switch, and it means editing code.

choices.text: A `default_headers` value asking the API to include debug details in each response
choices.reason: Default headers set request headers, and the SDK warns that overriding them can cause undefined behaviour; logging uses `ANTHROPIC_LOG`.

takeaway: Turn on the Python SDK's logs with **`ANTHROPIC_LOG=debug`** (or `info`); no code change needed.

stem: A voice assistant on Claude Opus 5.5 feels slow because users wait a long time before the first word arrives; once text starts, it streams quickly enough. A teammate proposes fast mode. What should the team expect?

choices.text: A big cut in that initial wait, since fast mode makes time to first token up to 2.5x faster
choices.reason: The up to 2.5x gain is in output tokens per second. The docs say fast mode's benefits are focused on OTPS, not time to first token.

choices.text: Not much help there: fast mode's gains are in output tokens per second, not time to first token
choices.reason: Correct: fast mode's speed benefits are focused on output tokens per second (OTPS), not time to first token (TTFT), so the initial wait isn't what it improves.

choices.text: A faster first word, because fast mode swaps in a smaller model that can start generating sooner
choices.reason: Fast mode runs the same model with a faster inference configuration: same weights and behavior, not a different model.

choices.text: No effect at all, because fast mode only applies to requests sent through the Message Batches API
choices.reason: It's the other way round: fast mode is not available with the Batch API. It works on regular requests, and its gain is most visible when streaming.

stem: A product manager hesitates to enable fast mode on Claude Opus 5.5 for a coding assistant, worried that answers will get worse in exchange for the extra speed. What is accurate?

choices.text: Quality drops a little, because fast mode runs a distilled copy of the model at lower effort
choices.reason: Fast mode keeps the same model weights and behavior; the docs say there is no change to intelligence or capabilities.

choices.text: Quality holds, and fast mode is billed at standard rates while it is in research preview
choices.reason: Fast mode is billed at premium pricing: $8 / $40 per MTok input / output on Claude Opus 5.5.

choices.text: Quality is unchanged: it's the same model on a faster inference setup, at a premium price
